article.text:
Run smarter agents. Use fewer tokens.
Our code review bill went up 36x this year. Now a review costs us 18 cents. See how ↓
 
Quickstart ·
Case studies ·
Tour ·
Templates ·
Deploy ·
Docs
AgentRun is an open-source platform that supercharges your agents. It adds self-improvement, durable execution and a
control plane on top of your favorite agent harness. Your agents become smarter, more fault tolerant and use fewer
tokens with every run.
An agent's Learning tab: what it kept, and what changed since. Demo data from the console's recorded fixtures.
## Case studies
**Code review.** Greptile started charging a dollar a review in March, then our agents took off, and our bill went
from $180 a month to $6,451. So we built our own reviewer on a cheap model and tuned it on our own PRs. It costs 18 cents a review, and on 30 PRs
it had never seen it caught 1.6x the real bugs Greptile did. [How we built it](docs/case-studies/code-review.md) · [Tune one on your repo](docs/tutorials/tune-a-template.md)
**Merchant codes.** We let Opus figure out how to classify merchants, then handed what it learned to a cheap model.
Same job, $0.89 down to $0.12 a merchant. [How it works](docs/case-studies/merchant-classification.md) · [Do it with your own job](docs/tutorials/learn-then-hand-off.md)
## Why AgentRun
Agents are great at figuring things out. The problem is they figure out the same things over and over. Give an agent
a job it has done a hundred times and it rediscovers the same API, rereads the same docs and rebuilds the same plan, and
you pay for every token of it.
Bring your agent on the harness it runs best on: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or pi. AgentRun does everything around it:
- **It learns the work.** After each run, the agent keeps what will help next time: a note, a skill, or a workflow
that does the job without the loop. The next run starts from there.
- **It never loses a run.** Every run lives in one store. Kill the server mid-run, start it again, and the run carries
on. Give each agent the computer the job needs: a sandbox, a Linux desktop, an Android phone or a browser.
- **You stay in control.** Approvals, spend caps and one console for every agent: what needs you, what failed, what's
running and what it cost.
You don't build the plumbing: provider integrations, recovery, run tracking and learning are all here. Run it on your
laptop with one command, in one container, or as a server with runners. Apache-2.0.
## Start in three steps
You need Node 24.22.3 or newer, on macOS or Linux.
1. **Start it.**
```sh
npx @parcha/agentrun
```
It starts the server and one runner on port 7340 (or the next free one), keeps everything in `~/.agentrun`, and
opens the console in your browser.
2. **Add one model key.** In the console, set a password, then add a key under **Settings → Model keys**. One
`OPENROUTER_API_KEY` gives every harness a model. An Anthropic key runs pi and Claude Code; an OpenAI key runs pi,
Codex and OpenCode.
3. **Run your first agent.** Open **Templates**, apply **KYB due diligence**, and start a run with a company's name and
website. It needs nothing but your model key. When it finishes, the run's **Report** tab has a due diligence report
with a verdict and every claim cited. Then open the agent's **Learning** tab to see what it kept for next time.
Rather have your coding agent do it? Tell it: `Read agentrun.ai/SKILL.md and set up AgentRun for me`.
Docker, sandboxes and running it on a server
If Docker is running on your machine, new agents get a Docker sandbox with a shell. Its image builds on first use,
which takes a few minutes, and the console says when it's ready. Without Docker, agents still read and write files,
but get no shell.
Want your own server with a URL? [Deploy it to Render](#deploy-it) in one click.
## Take the tour
**Workflows that make the call.** A step can ask a fast typed question, see how sure the answer is, and pick a route.
Here the model leans approve at 0.61, below the workflow's 0.75 bar,…

Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
The Antigravity Team
·Nov 12, 2026·3 min read
Share on XShare on BlueskyShare on LinkedIn
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency.
Selecting Orchestrator (Carbon) from the model selector in Google Antigravity.
Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator
Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems.
For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.
Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.
Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks.
Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation.

In this article
Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows.
While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, the Gemini app, Google Search, and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity.
Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.
Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads
In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.
To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.
Scaling developer and enterprise workflows
Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows:
Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash.

article.title: Introducing Claude Meetings, now in beta | Claude by Anthropic
article.text:
Introducing Claude Meetings
Add Claude to your video call and get the work started while you talk
CategoryProduct updates
DateNovember 12, 2026
Reading time5 min
Share
Claude can now join your video calls as a visible participant, follow the conversation and start on work during the meeting. Claude Meetings is now in beta.
Your team can ask Claude questions during the meeting, out loud or in chat. By default, Claude answers in writing, and it can use your connected tools with your permission.
Claude also works with you live to build docs, whiteboards (opens in new tab), or other artifacts, while teammates on the invite refine them. Claude writes the notes and action items, so no one on the call has to.
Claude Meetings is starting to roll out in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Support for other video conferencing platforms is coming soon.
What it looks like
Say your team is planning a customer event, and Claude is on the call. You say, “Claude, start a doc for this plan.” Claude writes up what the team has said so far, and teammates on the invite can edit the plan while you keep talking.
When you start discussing the budget, someone asks Claude what last year’s event cost. Claude asks for their approval to look it up, posts it in the meeting chat, and compares it to the current plan. When you start discussing timelines, someone asks Claude to put it on a whiteboard, and the team works on the schedule alongside the doc.
Before the meeting ends, someone asks Claude to share a recap with the team. After the call, any notes, action items, plan, and whiteboard are on the meeting’s page in claude.ai (opens in new tab).
Later, you can go back to meetings you were part of and ask Claude about them, or add Claude to the next one from your calendar in claude.ai.
We’re working with partners like Gong, Attention, Granola, Fireflies.ai, and Otter so you’ll soon be able to send a meeting’s transcript to the tools your team already uses.
Security and privacy
Claude adds a separate page for each meeting in claude.ai (opens in new tab) with the notes, transcript, and anything it built. People from your organization on the invite can see it and edit what Claude made, and it can be shared with others in your organization from the page.
By default, Claude is set to stay out of calls when someone from outside your organization is invited, and to leave if someone from outside joins partway through. An admin can allow Claude on calls with outside guests. On those calls, Claude posts its notice in the call’s chat but doesn’t reply there, and what guests say is included in the notes and transcript.
Claude uses each person’s connected tools with that person’s permission. It asks the first time, and a yes applies going forward. For now, when someone asks out loud, Claude asks each time to confirm who’s speaking. An answer posted in the call’s chat is visible to everyone on the call.
When Claude joins, it appears as a participant and posts a notice in the call’s chat. It saves a transcript, summary, and screen descriptions, not audio.
Before you add Claude or turn on auto-join, make sure everyone on your calls is OK with being transcribed.
Getting started
Claude joins when someone adds it or has auto-join on. Support is currently available for Google Meet, with other platforms coming soon. On Team plans, inviting Claude to your meetings is available by default, and an admin can turn it off. On Enterprise plans, an admin turns it on for all or part of the organization. While it’s in beta, it isn’t available to some organizations, including those with zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).
During the beta, Claude’s notes and transcripts are free on Team and Enterprise plans. So are its answers in your calls, unless an answer uses one of your connected tools, which counts toward your plan’s usage. The docs, whiteboards, (opens in new tab) and other artifacts Claude makes in a call are free…

About model
Inkling 2 Small has 594B parameters, 17B active parameters and a 1M-token context window. On Together AI it costs $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $1.00 per 1M output tokens.
Inkling 2 Small is the first model in Thinking Machines Lab's second Inkling generation: a Mixture-of-Experts model with 594B total parameters and 17B active per token, native image input, a 1M-token context window, and variable reasoning effort. It is more capable across the board than the first generation, particularly in long-horizon autonomous work, with gains in agentic coding, vision, knowledge work, and reasoning that come from improvements at every stage of training, including more efficient pre-training run natively in NVFP4 and a single large, unified reinforcement learning run. The model uses vision in the loop to interpret and refine the websites, games, and 3D designs it builds, handles finance and legal work over spreadsheets, filings, and documents, and is designed to respond well to fine-tuning, learning faster than Inkling Small on the same data. Released under Apache 2.0. Available on Together AI.

article.title: Foundation Models framework - Apple Developer
article.text:
Get started with the Foundation Models framework
The Foundation Models framework is the best way to use any large language model in your app. Whether you’re generating a quick summary or creating dynamic agents, the framework has what you need.
Overview
The Foundation Models framework is a native Swift API for integrating any large language model into your app — including direct access to the Apple Foundation Models on-device and in Private Cloud Compute. Powerful capabilities like guided generation, tool calling, image understanding, and Dynamic Profiles are built in, so you have what you need to build unique experiences.
What’s new in the Foundation Models framework
Meet the Foundation Models framework
Foundation Models framework
Human Interface Guidelines for Generative AI
Image understanding
Multimodal prompts let you pass images alongside text so your app can reason about visual content. This opens up new categories of experiences you can build with image understanding — it's as simple as attaching an image to your prompt. The Vision framework is also integrated directly, giving your model purpose-built tools like OCR for precise text extraction and barcode readers for quick code scanning — all on-device.
What’s new in image understanding
Model support
The Foundation Models framework gives you direct access to the on-device foundation model at the core of Apple Intelligence so you can build experiences that are smart, private, and work without internet connectivity.
On-device models are highly useful for many tasks, yet sometimes you need a larger model for a more complex workflow. The Foundation Models framework now extends to server models — like Claude, Gemini, and more — all through the same Swift API, with full support for features like tool calling and guided generation. Any model provider can create a Swift package conforming to the Language Model protocol, a fundamental component of the framework that allows you to pick the right language model for your app.
Supported third-party models
Core AI Language Models
MLX Language Models
Claude
Gemini
Private Cloud Compute
For those just getting started, developers who are enrolled in the App Store Small Business Program and have fewer than two million first-time App Store downloads can access the Apple Foundation Models running on Private Cloud Compute with no cloud API cost.* This delivers frontier-level intelligence with unparalleled privacy protections, ensuring that your users' data is not stored or accessible to Apple or anyone else.
Learn more about Private Cloud Compute
Build with the new Apple Foundation Model on Private Cloud Compute
Bring an LLM provider to the Foundation Models framework
Dynamic Profiles
Dynamic Profiles are new declarative APIs for continuously updating your session's model, tools, and instructions on the fly. Rather than creating a session with a fixed configuration, you define profiles — each with its own model, temperature, reasoning level, and toolset — and swap between them within a single continuous session. The session transcript is shared across every profile switch, so your app gets more contextual intelligence with less prompting. Dynamic Profiles are designed to be adaptable building blocks: use them to build AI agents, skills, or any other high-level abstraction your app needs.

Evaluations framework
The Evaluations framework gives you the ability to test your prompts and validate that your intelligence-powered features work correctly across dynamic conditions, going beyond what unit tests alone can catch. Whether you're iterating on instructions, switching models, or tuning a Dynamic Profile, Evaluations gives you confidence that your app's behavior holds up before you ship.

article.title: Jane Street Blog - Our software engineering interviews are changing (a little)
article.text:
Our software engineering interviews are changing (a little)
Nov 02, 2026 |
3 min read
Share on Facebook
Share on Twitter
Share on LinkedIn
By: Matthew Saffer
Over the last few years, LLMs have changed how software gets built and that’s no different
for us at Jane Street. Most of our engineers now use them every day not only for writing
code, but also for reading, debugging, and reviewing code, and plenty of things that
aren’t code at all.
We’ve talked about this recently in a podcast on how we use AI in our
development, and in a
post on formal methods
that touches on how agentic coding is reshaping the way we work.
Our coding interviews haven’t changed, though. The questions we ask software engineers
today are the same style of question we’ve been asking for years: sit down with an
interviewer or two, program through a problem together, and talk as you go.
That style has served us well and the key goals remain the same: we want to see how you
solve problems, structure your work, communicate, and collaborate in the pursuit of
excellent software development. But the shape of the job has evolved, and we think our
interviews should evolve, too. As generating code has become arguably cheaper than ever,
other parts of the job have come to matter even more: taste about what to build, choosing
abstractions that last, and making sure what got built is actually correct, among other
things.
So this summer we started trialing some new kinds of interviews in our onsites for campus
candidates. Broadly, they involve less code-writing, and lean more higher-level, focusing
on software design, on verifying the quality, structure, and intention of code, and on
using LLMs to produce code. Most rounds will continue to be traditional coding
interviews, conducted without LLM assistance.
We know this sounds vague, but that’s intentional: the formats are still evolving, and
we’d rather not describe something in detail today that looks different in six months.
A few things worth knowing:
Not every onsite includes these new rounds yet, and when you come on-site we’ll give you
a heads-up about what to expect.
The rest of our process is unchanged. If you’ve read our earlier posts about
interviewing here,
they’re still accurate.
While we find LLMs incredibly valuable as part of our daily work, we also recognize that
not everyone has deep experience working with them. You shouldn’t feel like you need to
have a highly worked out methodology for working with agents in order to do well in our
process. In the end, we’re looking for people with great instincts for building
software, and we don’t feel like we need an LLM to evaluate that.
Different folks have integrated LLMs into their workflows in different ways and to
different degrees, and we don’t expect you to have a particular setup or to use them for
everything. What we care about is that you think clearly about the tools you use: what
they’re good at, where they fall short, and when to reach for something else.
As has been the case for some time, our more experienced candidates’ interviews will
continue to be more varied, featuring a range of interview styles, from producing
software to designing systems and discussing prior work.
As always, we’ll keep iterating, and we’ll write more when there’s more to say.
If you’re interested in working with us, apply on our
website!
Matthew joined Jane Street in 2013 as a software engineer, and works on
distributed systems infrastructure and productivity tooling. In his free
time he noodles with making music.
